clue.text: Trap king with fine forged blade

parts.note: to pen an animal is to trap or shut it in
K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: forged means hammered into a new shape, so the letters of the word fine are reshaped

explanation.surface: A blacksmith with a trapped monarch, hammering out a fine sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forged' rearranges FINE into NIFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A small folding pocket blade is exactly what this tool is; the clue uses the general word for a cutting edge.

clue.text: Pomp 50% reduced thanks to King Edward?

indicators.note: cut by half, so only the first half of the word pomp remains

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks

explanation.surface: The pomp surrounding a king trimmed by half.
explanation.walkthrough: King Edward is a popular British variety of potato; the question mark marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A King Edward is a well-known British variety of this vegetable, a definition by example.

clue.text: Ian's thrown up: was first to be hammered

indicators.note: in a down clue, thrown up means the name Ian is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: the name Ian is taken as written; the 's is short for 'is', a link
to have led is to have been first

explanation.surface: Ian, sick after coming first, is beaten in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown up' reverses IAN to NAI.
explanation.definitionFit: A nail that has been hammered in is driven home; the verb means fastened with a hammer.

clue.text: Writes no publication for teachers

parts.note: TES is the Times Educational Supplement, the British teachers' paper

explanation.surface: Someone who writes but has nothing published for educators.
explanation.walkthrough: The TES is a British weekly magazine for school teachers.
explanation.definitionFit: To jot down or record something in writing is to make a note of it, as a verb.

clue.text: Rock fan rule: everyone wears black here

indicators.note: rock means shake or upset, so the letters of fan rule are jumbled

explanation.surface: A rock fan's dress code: all black, like goths.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the music genre but shakes up FAN RULE.
explanation.definitionFit: Mourners traditionally dress in black at a burial service.

clue.text: Called over by head of department to get order

indicators.note: over says the word for called is turned back to front

parts.note: called means named, as in 'a man called Bob'

indicators.note: head of picks out the opening letter of department

explanation.surface: An employee summoned by the department head to receive instructions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns NAMED into DEMAN; 'head of' gives D from department.
explanation.definitionFit: To order something is to require it, and a demand is a firm request or command.

clue.text: Postholders?

parts.note: not people who hold a job, but items that hold mail, letters sent by post

explanation.definitionFit: Paper wrappers contain letters for mailing, so they literally hold the post.

clue.text: Any gin? No? Awfully tiresome

indicators.note: awfully suggests something done badly, so those letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Being told there's no gin left is dreadfully irritating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awfully' rearranges ANY GIN NO.
explanation.definitionFit: Something irritating or vexing is tiresome.

clue.text: Walked out on sweet disheartened editor

indicators.note: disheartened means losing the heart, so the middle letter of the pudding word goes

parts.note: in British usage a sweet is a pudding or dessert

explanation.surface: A disappointed editor abandoned by someone over pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' takes the central S from DESSERT.
explanation.definitionFit: To have abandoned a partner is to have walked out on them.

clue.text: Perhaps Oliver in meeting with government's leader, spinning

parts.note: Oliver Twist is the Dickens orphan, so Oliver is an example of someone with the surname Twist

indicators.note: the leader of government's is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Oliver attends a meeting alongside the head of government, perhaps putting a spin on things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'meeting with' only joins the pieces; 'Perhaps' flags that Oliver is one example bearing the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe turning round and round, as a top or dancer rotates.

clue.text: Steven set off matches

indicators.note: set off suggests sending the letters away in a new arrangement, rearranging the name Steven

explanation.surface: A man named Steven heads off to watch some sporting fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set off' rearranges STEVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Sporting contests or fixtures are matches, the sense used on a sports programme.

clue.text: Bite lip

definitions.meaning: sharpness, as in a voice with bite or with an ... to it
the rim or brink, as in the lip of a cup

explanation.definitionFit: Both keenness, as in a sharp tone, and a border or rim, as of a cliff.

clue.text: Walk around certain to be adored

indicators.note: around says the word for walk is wrapped about the word for certain

parts.note: to tread is to walk or step
certain means sure

explanation.surface: Taking a walk with someone you are certain to love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walk' looks like the start of an instruction but is just a synonym; 'around' wraps it about the word for certain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something deeply loved and cherished is held dear like a precious possession.

clue.text: Film actor leaving quietly

indicators.note: leaving says the letter for quietly goes away from the word for actor

parts.note: an actor is a player on stage
P is the musical abbreviation for piano, quietly

explanation.surface: An actor slipping quietly off a film set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like the movie world but means a thin coating.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin coating or sheet over a surface is a film, such as a film of dust.

clue.text: Examination for all? Just some

indicators.note: Just some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Asking whether a test is open to everyone, or only to a few.
explanation.definitionFit: A spoken test, such as a language viva, is an examination conducted by speech rather than writing.

clue.text: Testimonial from first choice beginning to be ignored

indicators.note: the opening letter of the first-choice word is ignored, dropped

parts.note: a preference is the option you choose first

explanation.surface: A job applicant's testimonial ignored despite being the first choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to be ignored' drops P from PREFERENCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A testimonial from a past employer supporting a job applicant is called this.

clue.text: Cost created by former lover with writer, she being vacuous

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
a pen is a writing implement

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word she loses its middle and keeps only its outer letters

explanation.surface: A costly break-up involving an ex, an author and an empty-headed woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being vacuous' empties SHE to SE.
explanation.definitionFit: What something costs you is an outlay, a charge or payment.

clue.text: Wrapped up sailor thus, right before bed

indicators.note: before says the right letter comes ahead of bed

parts.note: AB is an able-bodied seaman, a sailor
so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: A sailor tucked up snugly before turning in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrapped up' hints at blankets but means engrossed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone deeply engrossed in a task is wrapped up in it, totally engaged.

clue.text: In carriage, for example

parts.note: carriage means posture or bearing, the way one holds oneself

explanation.surface: Inside a horse-drawn carriage, say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carriage' looks like a vehicle but means how a person stands.
explanation.definitionFit: A case or specimen used to illustrate something is an example, as in 'for instance'.

clue.text: Grumble about North — it gets payout from government

indicators.note: about says the word for grumble goes around the letter for North

parts.note: to beef is slang for to complain or grumble
N is the compass abbreviation for North

explanation.surface: Complaining about the North until it receives state handouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts N inside BEEF.
explanation.definitionFit: State welfare payments, such as unemployment allowance, are called this in Britain.

clue.text: Lorry driver finally mislaid food

indicators.note: mislaid means lost, so that closing letter goes missing from the vehicle

parts.note: a lorry is the British word for a truck

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of driver

explanation.surface: A lorry driver who has lost the packed lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' takes R from driver; 'mislaid' drops it from TRUCK. Tuck is British schoolboy slang for snacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuck is British informal slang for food, especially snacks and sweets at school.

clue.text: 'Reposez' primarily is French for 'stand'

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of Reposez is taken

parts.note: est is French for is

explanation.surface: A French language lesson translating a drill-sergeant's command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reposez' is French for 'rest', which makes the clue nearly self-explaining.
explanation.definitionFit: A support for something, such as a stand for a snooker cue or arm, is called by this name.

clue.text: Upset about poetry

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as in a letter heading
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Someone distressed by a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as distressed but means a defeat or setback.
explanation.definitionFit: A setback or reversal of fortune is an upset, as in a reverse on the battlefield.

clue.text: American fuel reprocessing is practical

parts.note: US stands for American, the United States

indicators.note: reprocessing means working over again, so the letters of fuel are rearranged

explanation.surface: Recycling American fuel is a sensible idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reprocessing' turns FUEL into EFUL.
explanation.definitionFit: Something serviceable that does a job well is practical.

clue.text: Tot was in the van, confused

parts.note: to tot up is to add
to be in the van, the vanguard, is to have led

explanation.surface: A small child riding in a van, bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' looks like a toddler but is the verb to add up; 'the van' is the vanguard, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A muddled, befuddled mind is described as confused.

clue.text: One lives by the river, that's comparatively warm in the East End

indicators.note: the Cockney accent of London's East End drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: comparatively warm means more warm, hotter

explanation.surface: A riverside creature, and an East Ender remarking that it's getting warmer.
explanation.walkthrough: The East End is a working-class part of London whose Cockney speech famously drops initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: This aquatic mammal makes its holt on riverbanks, so it is a riverside resident.

clue.text: 'Criminal is evil,' CID educated

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked or bent, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A detective's verdict that crime is wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: CID is Britain's police Criminal Investigation Department; 'Criminal' rearranges IS EVIL CID.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone refined, cultured and well brought up can be called educated in this sense.

clue.text: Everyone put up with mother's animal

indicators.note: in a down clue, put up means the word for everyone is written upwards

parts.note: everyone means all
ma is mother

explanation.surface: Everyone tolerated their mum's pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses ALL to LLA.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American pack beast is an example of an animal.

clue.text: Fruit — it could be crazy if you have more than one

definitions.text: it could be crazy if you have more than one
definitions.meaning: the plural is slang for mad or crazy

explanation.surface: A fruit that, if you collect several, can drive you mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow fruit, and its plural is the slang adjective meaning mad.

clue.text: Queen in a fuddle? Bad — very bad

indicators.note: bad tells us the letters are spoiled into a new order

parts.note: R is short for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A confused monarch's performance is judged terrible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges R, A and FUDDLE; 'very bad' is then the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something awful or terrible is very bad indeed.

clue.text: More intelligent animal restricts physical exercise

indicators.note: restricts means confines, so the animal word hems in the exercise letters

parts.note: a deer is an animal
PE is physical education or exercise at school

explanation.surface: A cleverer creature that limits its own workouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricts' says the animal word holds the exercise abbreviation; PE is the school subject of physical education.
explanation.definitionFit: A more profound thinker is described this way, as having more depth of thought.

clue.text: Comprehensive education's flipping pursued

indicators.note: flipping means turned over, so the education letters run backwards

parts.note: ED is the abbreviation for education
to tail someone is to follow or pursue them

explanation.surface: A grumble that comprehensive-school education has been hounded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comprehensive' suggests a British state school but means thorough; 'flipping' turns ED into DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough, full account covering every particular is comprehensive.
